column2: Fees should be given in all sacrifices by one wishing prosperity, and costly household sacrifices should be performed by all robbers.
These duties, of such kinds, were ordained of old, blameless one, and are to be performed here by the whole world, lord of the earth.
Robbers are seen in the world among all classes, men living in other signs of life, even in all four stages.
When the rod-policy is lost and the dharma of kings is cast aside, beings are bewildered through the wickedness of kings, O king.
Beggars and wearers of badges will be countless, and the variations of the stages of life, when this Krita age ends.
Not hearing the best courses of the ancient dharmas, impelled by desire and anger, they will take the wrong path.
When sin is turned back by the great souls with the rod-policy, then dharma, being the eternal highest, does not waver.
One who scorns the king, the teacher of the next world, finds that nothing he gives, offers or does for ancestors ever bears fruit.
The gods too greatly honour the lord of men, the eternal, god-like king who loves dharma.
The revered Prajapati who created the whole world desires the kshatriya order for the promotion and restraint of dharmas.
One who by his understanding remembers the course of dharma that has been set in motion is to be honoured and revered by me; in that the kshatriya order is established.
Having said this, the revered lord, surrounded by hosts of Maruts, Vishnu, went to his abode, the imperishable supreme station.
With dharma so set in motion of old and well practised, blameless one, who would scorn the kshatriya, if he had thought and much learning?
What is begun and ended wrongly dissolves in the middle, like a blind man on the road.
As the wheel was first set in motion, so with the first as the refuge, act, tiger among men; I know you, blameless one."

All dharmas are known here to you, Yudhishthira, as they are known to me, mighty-armed one, approved by the good.
mahabharata:12:66.3	But what you ask me, Yudhishthira, concerning the dharma of those gone to other signs, best of upholders of dharma, hear that, lord of men.
mahabharata:12:66.4	All these, son of Kunti, exist for those engaged in good conduct and the works of the four stages, bull among men.
mahabharata:12:66.5	For one free of desire and aversion, by the rod-policy, Yudhishthira, regarding all beings equally, the station of the alms-life is his.
mahabharata:12:66.6	One who knows taking and giving, restraint and favour, a hero of the conduct as stated, has the station of the stage of security.
mahabharata:12:66.7	For one who lifts up kinsmen, relatives and friends who have fallen into misfortune, the station of the stage of initiation is his.
mahabharata:12:66.8	For one who performs the daily rites, offerings to beings, offerings to ancestors and to men on a great scale, Partha, the station of the forest stage is his.
mahabharata:12:66.9	By protecting all beings and ruling his own kingdom, the king's manifold initiation is the station of the forest stage.
mahabharata:12:66.11	For one who follows a straight and honest path always toward all beings, the station of the Brahma stage is his.
mahabharata:12:66.12	For one giving abundant wealth to forest-dwelling Brahmanas and those learned in the three Vedas, the station of the forest stage is his.
mahabharata:12:66.13	For one who shows compassion to all beings, engaged in kindness, there is a station in every condition.
mahabharata:12:66.14	For one who shows compassion toward children and the aged, Kaurava, Yudhishthira, there is a station in every condition.
mahabharata:12:66.15	Protecting beings that have been wronged by force, delight of the Kurus, and those who seek refuge, Kaurava, one would dwell in the householder's life.
mahabharata:12:66.16	Protecting all moving and unmoving beings in every way and always honouring as is fitting, one would dwell in the householder's life.
mahabharata:12:66.17	Restraint and favour toward the elder, the younger, wives, brothers, sons and grandsons, Partha—that is the householder's life, that is austerity.
mahabharata:12:66.18	Protecting the good, who are worthy of honour, among the subjects, whose selves are known—that would be the station of the householder's stage.
mahabharata:12:66.19	One who in his house takes with food all those who dwell in stages, that is the householder's life, Yudhishthira.
mahabharata:12:66.20	A man established in the dharma made by the Creator as it truly is gains the unsurpassed fruit of all the stages.
mahabharata:12:66.21	In whom virtues never perish, son of Kunti, him too, the best of men, they call one who dwells in a stage, Yudhishthira.
mahabharata:12:66.22	Showing regard for rank, age and family, one dwells in all the stages, Yudhishthira.
mahabharata:12:66.23	Protecting the dharmas of countries, son of Kunti, and the dharmas of families, tiger among men, a king would be one of all stages.
mahabharata:12:66.24	Honouring in due season the prosperity of beings and the offerings, tiger among men, he would dwell in the stage of the good.
mahabharata:12:66.25	One who, having gone ten ways of dharma, looks to the dharma of the whole world, son of Kunti, becomes a king in a stage.
mahabharata:12:66.26	Those skilled in dharma in the world, the good who practise dharma, protected in the domain of a lord of the earth—a quarter share of that dharma is his.
mahabharata:12:66.27	Kings who do not protect men who delight in dharma and are devoted to dharma, tiger among men—those men take away their sin.
mahabharata:12:66.28	And those who are the helpers in protection of kings, Yudhishthira, all share in the portion of dharma done, blameless one.
mahabharata:12:66.29	In all the stations of the stages, they say, the householder's life is bright in its decision, a purifier, tiger among men, which we worship.
mahabharata:12:66.30	The man who is like himself toward beings, who has laid down the rod and conquered anger, gains happiness after death.
mahabharata:12:66.31	A swift boat, risen from dharma, strong in sattva, with dharma as its bridge and banyan, with renunciation as wind on its way, will carry you across.
mahabharata:12:66.32	When all desire that was in his heart has turned back, then he becomes established in sattva and thence attains Brahma.
mahabharata:12:66.33	Very serene by feeling and by yoga, lord of men, you will attain dharma, tiger among men, delighting in protection.
mahabharata:12:66.34	Make effort in protecting the Brahmanas who study the Veda, doers of good deeds, and all the world, blameless one.
mahabharata:12:66.35	The dharma that one practises in the forest and in the stages, Bharata, a king obtains a hundredfold by protection.
mahabharata:12:66.36	This manifold dharma has been declared to you, best of the Pandavas; follow it, seen by the ancients, eternal.
mahabharata:12:66.37	With one-pointed mind in the four stages and the four classes, Pandava, you will attain dharma, tiger among men, delighting in protection.

The most necessary task of a kingdom is the consecration of a king; a kingdom without Indra is weak, and robbers overpower it.
mahabharata:12:67.3	In kingdoms without a king dharma does not stand firm, and they devour one another; fie on kinglessness in every way.
mahabharata:12:67.4	The scripture says they chose this one as Indra, the king; as Indra, so the king is to be honoured by one wishing prosperity.
mahabharata:12:67.5	The Vedic rule is that one should not dwell in kingdoms without a king; in kingdoms without a king even Fire does not carry the oblation.
mahabharata:12:67.6	And if one seeking the kingdom, stronger, should come against kingdoms without kings or with kings slain,
mahabharata:12:67.7	he should be met and honoured; this is well counselled here; for there is nothing worse than sin, nothing worse than kinglessness.
mahabharata:12:67.8	If he were to see rightly, all would be well; for a strong man enraged might even make an end entirely.
mahabharata:12:67.9	A cow that is hard to milk suffers much trouble; but they do not trouble one that milks easily.
mahabharata:12:67.10	What is not heated bends, they do not heat it; and wood that has itself bowed they do not bend further.
mahabharata:12:67.11	By this likeness the wise should bow to the stronger; one who bows to the stronger bows to Indra.
mahabharata:12:67.12	Therefore a king must always be made by one wishing prosperity; neither wealth nor wife is for those who have no king.
mahabharata:12:67.13	A sinner seizing another's wealth in a kingless land is pleased; but when others take from him, then he wishes for a king.
mahabharata:12:67.14	Even sinners then never get safety; for one is robbed by two, and two by many others.
mahabharata:12:67.15	A non-slave is made a slave, and women are taken by force; for this reason the gods made rulers of subjects.
mahabharata:12:67.16	If there were no king in the world and no rod-bearer on earth, the stronger would roast the weaker on a spit like fish.
mahabharata:12:67.17	We have heard that in the beginning kingless peoples perished, eating one another like fish in water the thin ones.
mahabharata:12:67.18	Assembling, they then made agreements, we have heard: One who is harsh in speech, violent, an adulterer, or does not take his own—we shall abandon such."
To give confidence to all classes without distinction, they made an agreement, but did not stay by the agreement.
Together they then went to the Grandsire, afflicted with unhappiness: "Lordless, we perish, revered one; appoint a lord for us,
whom we may worship together and who may protect us." He directed Manu for them, but Manu did not welcome them.
I fear the cruel work; kingship is exceedingly hard, especially among men always of false conduct.
The subjects said to him: "Do not fear; sin will not go to you for the work. We shall give you a fiftieth of animals and of gold, and a tenth of grain, to increase the treasury.
Those men who are mainly chief with weapon and wing will follow you, like gods Mahendra.
You, having gained strength, king, hard to assail and glorious, will place us all in happiness as Kubera does the Nairritas.
And a fourth of whatever dharma the subjects, well protected by the king, practise will rest with you for us.
Nourished by that great dharma, won easily, protect us on all sides, king, as Shatakratu the gods.
Go out swiftly to victory, blazing like the sun with rays; crush the pride of your enemies; may dharma always conquer for us."
He set out, greatly radiant, surrounded by a great army, endowed with noble birth, blazing as it were with splendour.
Seeing his greatness, like the gods seeing Mahendra's, all were terrified and set their minds on their own dharma.
Then he went round the earth like a raining cloud, calming sins everywhere and engaging them in their own works.
Thus those men on earth who wish prosperity should first make a king, for the favour of the subjects.
And they should bow to him in devotion as pupils to a teacher always, as the gods to the thousand-eyed, the subjects to the king near them.
One honoured by his own people here is greatly esteemed by others; but one slighted by his own people is despised by others.
Contempt of the king by others brings unhappiness to all; therefore umbrella, leaf-fan, garments, ornaments,
foods and drinks, houses, seats, beds and all equipment they should give to the king.
He should be guarded in himself, hard to assail, speaking first with a smile, and when addressed he should answer men sweetly.
Grateful, firm in devotion, a sharer, with senses subdued, when looked at he should look back, gently, honestly and pleasantly."

Here too they recite this ancient history, how Vasumanas questioned Brihaspati, Bharata.
mahabharata:12:68.3	A king named Vasumanas, Kausalya, best of the wise, of trained understanding, questioned the great sage Brihaspati.
mahabharata:12:68.4	Having done all the observances of discipline, knowing discipline, turning to the right of Brihaspati and bowing duly,
mahabharata:12:68.5	delighting in the welfare of all beings, wishing the good of the subjects, he asked the rule of kingship, the root of dharma, lord of men.
mahabharata:12:68.6	By what do beings flourish and by what do they decline? Honouring whom, great sage, would they attain utmost happiness?"
Thus asked by the great king Kausalya of immeasurable splendour, Brihaspati calmly told him of the honouring of kings.

The dharma of the world is seen to be rooted in the king, great king; the subjects do not eat one another only from fear of the king.
mahabharata:12:68.9	The king pacifies by dharma the whole world, agitated and eager, and having pacified, shines.
mahabharata:12:68.14	The strong would seize the possessions of the weak and kill those who strive, if the king did not protect.
mahabharata:12:68.15	Sinners would suddenly seize vehicles, garments, ornaments and jewels of many kinds, if the king did not protect.
mahabharata:12:68.16	There would be no ownership in this world of this is mine"; universal ruin would set in, if the king did not protect.
They would torment or even kill mother, father, the aged, teacher, guest and elder, if the king did not protect.
Weapons of many kinds would fall in many ways on those who practise dharma, and unrighteousness would be accepted, if the king did not protect.
Killing, binding and torment would ever befall the wealthy, and they would not know possession, if the king did not protect.
The world would end in the sky, be given over to robbers, and fall into dreadful hell, if the king did not protect.
Neither breeding nor agriculture nor trade routes would continue, dharma would sink and the triple learning would not be, if the king did not protect.
Sacrifices with proper fees would not proceed duly, nor marriages or assemblies, if the king did not protect.
Bulls would not run, churns would not churn, and cow-pens would perish, if the king did not protect.
Terrified, anguished in heart, crying "Alas", senseless, all would perish in a moment, if the king did not protect.
Year-long sacrificial sessions would not stand free of fear, with proper fees, if the king did not protect.
The ascetic Brahmanas would not study the four Vedas, though bathed in learning and bathed in austerity, if the king did not protect.
Hand would rob hand, all bridges would be broken, and all would flee in fear, if the king did not protect.
People struck down by the slain Brahmanas would find no union with dharma; the doer would go as his own senses wish, if the king did not protect.
Unjust acts would proceed, mixture of classes would occur, and famine would enter the kingdom, if the king did not protect.
Men, protected by the king, sleep as they please with their house doors open, fearless on every side.
No one tolerates abuse, how much less a hand raised, if the king is a righteous protector of men.
Women without men, adorned with all ornaments, travel the road fearless when the lord of the earth protects.
They follow dharma only and do not injure one another, and favour one another, when the lord of the earth protects.
The three classes sacrifice with great sacrifices of various kinds and study scripture with application, when the lord of the earth protects.
This world is rooted in trade and ever held up by the triple learning; all that proceeds rightly when the lord of the earth protects.
When the king takes the best of burdens and bears the subjects with great exercise of force, then the world is content.
In whose absence beings would be absent on every side, and in whose presence there would be constant presence—who would not honour him?
One who carries his burden, which brings happiness to all the world, should remain devoted to the king's welfare; he would conquer both worlds.
Any man who would even in mind think of sin against him will surely suffer here and fall into hell after death.
A king must never be scorned as a mere man; for this is a great deity standing in human form.
He takes on five forms joined to times: he becomes Fire, Sun, Death, Vaishravana and Yama.
When he burns sinners with fierce splendour, wrongly served, then the king becomes Fire.
When the king sees all beings through spies and goes after making good, then he becomes the Sun.
When, angry, he destroys by hundreds the impure men with their sons, grandsons and ministers, then he becomes the Ender.
When he restrains all the unrighteous with sharp rods and favours the righteous, then he becomes Yama.
When he satisfies benefactors with streams of wealth and takes away the many jewels of wrongdoers,
gives fortune to one and takes it from another, then the king, O king, becomes Vaishravana in the world.
One should not stay in disparagement of him, a skilled man of untroubled deeds, wishing lawful gain, without envy of the lord.
One who does what is hostile to the king would not get happiness, even if a son, brother or friend equal to himself.
Fire, blazing, with the wind as charioteer, might leave a remainder; but for one attacked by the king no remainder exists anywhere.
One should avoid from afar all things guarded by him, and be as repelled by seizing the king's property as by death.
One who lays hands on it soon perishes, as a deer touching a snare; a wise man should guard the king's property as his own.
The senseless who seize the king's wealth fall for a long time into great, dreadful, groundless hell.
King, Bhoja, Virat, Samrat, Kshatriya, Bhupati, Nripa—who would not wish to honour him who is praised by such words?
Therefore one wishing prosperity, restrained, self-conquered, with senses subdued, intelligent, mindful and skilled, should resort to the lord of the earth.
A king should honour a minister who is grateful, wise, not petty, firm in devotion, with senses subdued, ever devoted to dharma and steady in position.
He should rely on a man of firm devotion, trained intellect, who knows dharma, is self-restrained, brave, of non-petty deeds, one who avoids crowds.
A king makes a man bold; a king strengthens a thin man; how can one attacked by the king have happiness? A king makes a man who approaches him happy.
The king is the weightier heart of the subjects, their refuge, foundation and supreme happiness; relying on him men rightly win this world and the next, the lord of men.
The lord of men too, having governed the earth by self-control, truth and friendliness, and having sacrificed with great sacrifices, the greatly renowned one attains an honoured place in heaven."
Thus instructed by his teacher, Kausalya, the best of kings, the hero, with effort protected the subjects.

How should he employ spies, how win the confidence of the classes, how treat servants, wives and sons, Bharata?
mahabharata:12:69.3	Hear attentively the whole conduct of kings, great king; what is to be done first by a king, or by a lord of the earth.

The self is always to be conquered by the king; then enemies are to be conquered. How could a king who has not conquered himself conquer foes?
mahabharata:12:69.5	This is self-conquest: restraint of the five groups; a king with senses subdued can oppress enemies.
mahabharata:12:69.6	He should post garrisons in forts and at borders, delight of the Kurus, in the town's gardens and in the city's parks,
mahabharata:12:69.7	in all stations and cities, in the middle of the city, tiger among men, and in the royal residence.
mahabharata:12:69.8	Then he should post agents in the guise of the dull, blind and deaf, tested men, wise, able to bear hunger, thirst and heat.
mahabharata:12:69.9	Among all ministers, in the three kinds of friends, and among sons, great king, he should station them attentively.
mahabharata:12:69.12	In gardens and parks, at meetings of the learned, in brothels, at crossings, in assemblies and rest-houses.
mahabharata:12:69.13	Thus the wise man should defeat the enemy's agents by agents; all that is struck by spies is struck, Pandava.
mahabharata:12:69.14	When a king knows himself to be weaker, he should consult with ministers and make peace with the stronger.
mahabharata:12:69.15	Not known to be weak, he should make peace with the enemy, or wishing some aim, the wise one should act swiftly.
mahabharata:12:69.16	The king should make peace with those who are virtuous, of great energy, knowers of dharma and good, while protecting the kingdom by dharma.
mahabharata:12:69.17	Knowing himself to be uprooted, the wise king should slay former wrongdoers and all who are hated by the world.
mahabharata:12:69.18	A king who can neither benefit nor harm, and is unable to raise himself, would be ignored.
mahabharata:12:69.19	The wise should march unannounced, without outcry, against the next, the engaged, the careless and the weak.
mahabharata:12:69.20	The hero should order the march when strong, well-fed, powerful and at ease, having first made arrangements for the march and in the city.
mahabharata:12:69.21	Even if that king is valiant, he should not be subject to him; but if he is deficient in strength and valour, he should dwell near and weaken him.
mahabharata:12:69.22	He should oppress his kingdom by weapons, fire, poison and stupefaction, and cause disputes among the ministers and favourites; war should always be avoided by a wise man wishing kingdom.
mahabharata:12:69.23	Brihaspati says gain of wealth is by three means: conciliation, gifts and division, O lord of men; by whichever he can obtain the aim, the wise man should be content.
mahabharata:12:69.24	He should take a tax from the subjects, delight of the Kurus, one sixth, being of immeasurable wisdom, for their very protection.
mahabharata:12:69.25	From those who have gone ten dharma-ways, whether much or little wealth, he should not take suddenly, for the protection of the townsfolk.
mahabharata:12:69.26	The townsfolk are to be regarded as sons, without doubt; devotion to them should be shown in showing the dealings.
mahabharata:12:69.27	A king should establish a son who sees all aims in the courts, for the kingdom stands on legal dealings constantly.
mahabharata:12:69.28	At mines, salt, tolls, ferries and elephant forests, a king should post ministers or his own trusted men, well-wishers.
mahabharata:12:69.29	A king who rightly bears the rod always attains dharma; the rod of a king, rightly applied, is praised in dharma.
mahabharata:12:69.30	A king should be learned in the Vedas and their limbs, wise, a great ascetic, ever generous and given to sacrifice, Bharata.
[Death said:] "Therefore we both are under Time's sway and doers of what is fated; we are never to be blamed by you, hunter."
He had a hundred sons, O king, supremely righteous; and Ikshvaku, the lord, made all of them lords of the earth.
Then Dhritarashtra assembled his friends and, with his voice greatly choked with tears, said these words:
In Krishna's presence Rama with Kritavarman drank, and Yuyudhana, Gada and Babhru likewise.
Ho, king, look: I have fallen, dear to you; tell me, if you know, why I have fallen.
Not understanding those voices, Yudhishthira, son of Dharma, said: "Who are you, and why do you stay here?"
